### Causal reasoning under interference {#sec-causal-interference .unnumbered}

##### 

To conduct causal inference under interference, it necessary to have an idea which units can affect which other units, and a function for how that influence shapes the measures taken from each unit. 

##### Graphs {#sec-graphs}

Graphs give us a language to describe these interference structures. A graph represents units as nodes and possible pathways of influence between units as edges. Graphs help us represent who is “eligible” to affect whom. Potential outcomes can then be thought of as depending both on a unit’s own treatment and that of the units its directly connected to.

##### Network exposure mappings {#sec-exposure-mapping}

While graphs tell us who is connected, we need a way to incorporate information from the network in order to express counterfactual quantities. Network exposure mappings do this by turning the vector of neighbors’ treatments into a scalar quantity, such as the count or proportion of vaccinated neighbors. Together with graphs, exposure mappings allow us to formalize how interference operates: graphs define the structure of possible influence across units, while exposure mappings define how units incorporate that influence.  


##### Homogeneous network interference {#sec-homogeneous-interference}

We introduce the assumption of *homogeneous network interference* which reduces the complexity of network exposure mappings. This assumption holds that the effect of a neighbor’s treatment on unit $i$ is the same regardless of which neighbor it is, and regardless of the position of unit $i$ in the network. What matters is the *number* or *proportion* of treated neighbors, not their identity. Finally, it restricts the network exposure values so that they are contained by a finite set.
